objectives:
This course, joined by visiting professor Jason McGrath, traces the history of cinema on mainland China from the Republican Era in the 1920s-40s through the PRC (1949-present). The course closely follows the textbook Chinese Film: Realism and Convention from the Silent Era to the Digital Age (Jason McGrath, University of Minnesota Press, 2022), which is available in its entirety in an open-access digital edition that includes 80+ extra figures and embedded video clips for every scene discussed.

The focus is on films recognized for their artistic quality and/or historical significance. The central theme throughout the course and the textbook is the dialectical tension between realism(s) and convention(s), meaning the following:
•	Realism(s) – the various different claims made to realism throughout Chinese cinema history, from the ontological realism of the photographic image in early 1920s cinema, to the critical/social realism of the “Shanghai left-wing cinema movement” of the 1930s-40s, to the socialist realism of the Mao era, to the “post-socialist realism” of post-Mao China and the various forms of realism today, including the “capitalist realism” of some mainstream entertainment cinema and the “perceptual realism” of films with special effects from computer-generated imagery (CGI).
•	Convention(s) – the various norms of narrative, genre, and ideology that determine filmmaking in spite of any claims to representing reality itself, from the stage conventions of traditional Chinese opera, to the norms of storytelling and continuity borrowed from classical Hollywood narration, to the formulas of socialist realism inherited from the Soviet Union, to the conventions of neorealist cinema, to the contemporary conventions of “main melody cinema” (主旋律電影), action cinema, science fiction cinema, and so on.

On one hand, at each moment in film history, any claims to realism are mitigated by the conventions operative in filmmaking at that historical moment. On the other hand, the effect of realism is itself attained by applying techniques that can become conventionalized, so that styles of film narration that seem realist in one historical moment can appear formulaic in a later historical moment. We can thus trace the history of mainland Chinese cinema through the dialectic of realism and convention.

Learning Objectives:

For the purpose of education at the upper-division (advanced) undergraduate level, this course serves two main objectives:
1.	Teach the basic skills of film analysis, including how to accurately use the vocabulary for the description of mise-en-scene, cinematography, and editing. This is accomplished through a series of assignments: (a) frame analysis; (b) shot analysis; (c) scene analysis. These analytical skills then serve as the building blocks for making larger arguments of film interpretation, which occurs in later course assignments: (a) scene argument; (b) film motif argument; (c) narrative parallelism argument; (d) film interpretation.
2.	Trace the history of mainland Chinese cinema and explore what it teaches us about modern Chinese political, social, and cultural history. Every moment of cinema history takes place against the backdrop of Chinese history in general and thus can provide insight into that history.
content:
WEEK 1
Films:
Laborer's Love 勞工之愛情 (dir. Zhang Shichuan 張石川, 1922, 22 min）
Romance of the Western Chamber 西廂記 (dir. Hou Yao 侯曜, 1927, 45 min)
Readings:
Robert Spadoni, “Mise-en-scene” and “Cinematography,” (only until “Moving the Frame”) in A Pocket Guide to Analyzing Films, 71-88, 89-111.
Yale Film Analysis website – Basic Terms, Mise-en-scene, & Cinematography, only until Section 4–Movement）
McGrath, Chinese Film, “Intro – Inscribing the Real: Cinematic Realism and Convention”

WEEK 2
Film:
The Goddess 神女, dir. Wu Yonggang 吳永剛, 1934, 79 min)
Readings:
McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 1 “Acting Real in Chinese Silent Cinema” (pp. 33-48; until “Film vs. Stage Performance” section)

WEEK 3
Film:
Centre Stage 阮玲玉 (dir. Stanley Kwan 關錦鵬, 1991, 126 min)
Reading:
McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 1 “Acting Real in Chinese Silent Cinema” (pp. 48-69; from “Film vs. Stage Performance” section to end of chapter)

WEEK 4
Film:
Crossroads 十字街頭, Shen Xiling 沈西苓, 1937, 104 min）
Reading:
Reading: McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 2 “Shanghaiing Hollywood in the 1930s” (pp. 71-92; until “Undermining Elevation: Street Angel” section)
Robert Spadoni, “Cinematography,” in A Pocket Guide to Analyzing Films (U California Press, 2014), 111-120.
Yale Film Analysis website – Cinematography page, Section 4–Movement

WEEK 5
Film:
Street Angel 馬路天使, dir. Yuan Muzhi 袁牧之, 1937, 90 min)
Reading:
Reading: McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 2 “Shanghaiing Hollywood in the 1930s” (pp. 92-113; from “Undermining Elevation: Street Angel” section to end of chapter)

WEEK 6
Film:
Spring in a Small Town 小城之春, dir. Fei Mu 費穆, 1948, 93 min)
Reading:
McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 3 “Realism and Event in Postwar Chinese Cinema” (pp. 115-143; until “When Cinema and History Converge: Crows and Sparrows” section)

WEEK 7
Film:
Crows and Sparrows 烏鴉與麻雀, dir. Zheng Junli 鄭君里, 1949, 108 min）
Reading:
McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 3 “Realism and Event in Postwar Chinese Cinema” (pp. 144-157; from “When Cinema and History Converge: Crows and Sparrows” section to end of chapter)
Robert Spadoni, “Editing,” in A Pocket Guide to Analyzing Films, 121-150.

WEEK 8
Film:
The Song of Youth 青春之歌 (dir. Cui Wei & Chen Huai’ai, 1959, 180 min)
Reading:
McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 4 ”Prescriptive Realism in Revolutionary Cinema of the Seventeen Years” (pp. 159-180; until paragraph beginning “In sum,…”)
Yale Film Analysis website – Editing & Sound pages

WEEK 9
Film:
The Red Detachment of Women 紅色娘子軍 (dir. Xie Jin 謝晉, 1960）
Reading:
McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 4 ”Prescriptive Realism in Revolutionary Cinema of the Seventeen Years” (pp. 180-198; from paragraph beginning “In sum,…” to end of chapter)

WEEK 10
Film:
selected clips from 樣板戲 films:《智取威虎山》《紅燈記》《紅色娘子軍》《平原作戰》
Reading:
McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 5 ”Socialist Formalism and the End(s) of Revolutionary Cinema” (pp. 199-216; until “Formalism and Ideology” section)

WEEK 11
Film:
Guerrillas on the Plain (平原游擊隊; dir. Su Li 蘇裡 & Wu Zhaodi 武兆堤, 1955, 140 min)
Reading:
McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 5 ”Socialist Formalism and the End(s) of Revolutionary Cinema” (pp. 216-240; from “Formalism and Ideology” section to end of chapter)

WEEK 12
Film:
Yellow Earth 黃土地 (dir. Chen Kaige 陳凱歌, 1984, 92 min）
Reading:
McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 6 “A Long Take on Post-Socialist Realism,” (pp. 241-260; only until the section “Stylistic Neorealism”)

WEEK 13
Film:
Xiao Wu 小武 （dir. Jia Zhangke 賈樟柯, 1997, 99 min）
Reading:
Reading: McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 6 “A Long Take on Post-Socialist Realism,” (pp. 260-280; from “Stylistic Neorealism” section to end of chapter)

WEEK 14
Film:
The Wandering Earth 2 流浪地球 (dir. Guo Fan 郭帆, 2023, 173 min）
Reading:
McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 7 “Chinese Cinematic Realism(s) in the Digital Age” (pp. 281-303; only until the section “The Ontological Realism of the Digital Image”)

WEEK 15
Film:
The Mermaid 美人魚 (dir. Stephen Chow 周星馳, 2016, 94 min)
Reading:
McGrath, Chinese Film, ch 7 “Chinese Cinematic Realism(s) in the Digital Age” (pp. 304-318; from “The Ontological Realism of the Digital Image” section to end of chapter)
Reading: Robert Spadoni, “Film as Form,” in A Pocket Guide to Analyzing Films (U California Press, 2014), 7-46.

WEEK 16
Film:
Kaili Blues 路邊野餐 (dir. Bi Gan 畢贛, 2015, 94 min)
Reading:
McGrath, Chinese Film, “Conclusion” (pp. 319-328)
Reading: Robert Spadoni, “Narrative,” in A Pocket Guide to Analyzing Films (U California Press, 2014), 47-68.
books:
Jason McGrath. Chinese Film: Realism and Convention from the Silent Era to the Digital Age. Minneapolis: University of Minnesota Press, 2022.
Open access edition: https://manifold.umn.edu/projects/chinese-film
All other readings provided as PDF files or Internet links
